newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers move towards ending strike.
newsitem.headline: French truckers move towards ending strike.

text.p: A 12-day strike by French truck drivers blockading the country neared conclusion on Friday after unions signed an early retirement deal and consulted their members at roadblocks on ending the action.

All unions, including the hardline Communist-led CGT, said they had achieved substantial progress on the outstanding issues of pay and working hours in talks with road haulage employers and the government at the Transport Ministry.
Negotiators signed five agreements covering retirement at 55 instead of 60, sick pay, travel expenses, union rights and a ban on Sunday driving.
"Our feeling is that our profession has won dignity and recognition in these 12 days of struggle," CFDT spokesman Claude Debons told reporters.

Even as union leaders announced they would consult their members, truckers began voting with their wheels by lifting some of the blockades that had been strangling the economy in cities such as Arles and Avignon.
The strikers lifted a roadblock at the main Channel port of Calais, allowing stranded British and foreign trucks to board ferries for England, the Chamber of Commerce said.
But some 210 barricades remained in place on highways and at fuel depots against a peak of 249 on Thursday, leading to petrol rationing in almost half of the country.

Unions said the employers had doubled their offer of a special bonus payment to 3,000 francs ($600) in a bid to end the deadlock and the government promised to issue a decree on work time within two weeks, meeting a key demand for full payment for hours worked including unloading time and compulsory rest.
"It's up to the strikers on the roadblocks to decide," said Roger Poletti, head of the Force Ouvriere transport workers' union.
Government mediator Robert Cros said that Transport Minister Bernard Pons had instructed him to chair a supervisory committee "to ensure what is signed is actually implemented".

He said the government would put to the parties "in the coming hours for very rapid signature" a draft decree abolishing longstanding practices whereby truckers are paid for fewer hours than they actually work or are on standby.
"As for the definition of working time, the government has appointed me to to work out a solution by December 15 with the parties," Cros said. "This subject will also be the object of a decree."

On Thursday night, Prime Minister Alain Juppe urged a fast solution, cautioning that "the consequences (of a prolonged strike) on our economy, on many companies, on many workers risk being very damaging".
He ruled out using force to clear truckers' blockades.
Truckers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid as they wait to load and unload.
The strike, in the crucial pre-Christmas commercial period, has cost European food and haulage industries tens of millions of dollars a day, prompting protests from France's neighbours.
Truckers have also sealed off France's 13 oil refineries. Petrol rationing has spread and about 8,000 of 18,000 petrol stations were either dry or feeling shortages.

The roadblocks have forced the closures of some factories for lack of supplies and cut deliveries of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers. In Rouen, in Normandy, 9,000 workers from various sectors were temporarily laid off.
In London, Britain's Transport Secretary George Young summoned the French ambassador on Thursday to express concern over the stranding of British lorries, officials said.
The blockade has also stranded up to 14,000 Spanish trucks and idled about 90 percent of Portugal's total truck fleet. Belgian ports were clogged by British-bound lorries avoiding France.
